title: Alcohol and Running: Hangover Runs, Race Prep, and Recovery
excerpt: How alcohol affects running: whether to run with a hangover, how much to drink before a race, beer as recovery, and the warning signs that mean stop and get help.
metaDescription: How alcohol affects running: should you run hungover, how much to drink before a race, beer after a run, and the warning signs that mean stop.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol and running don't mix well, but they don't have to be enemies either. A drink or two the night before an easy run is unlikely to matter much for most healthy runners. The problems start with heavier drinking: it disrupts your sleep, adds to fluid loss, lowers blood sugar, slows muscle recovery, and leaves your heart working harder the next day. That combination makes hard workouts, long runs, and races noticeably tougher, and in hot weather it can become unsafe.

**The quick rules:** Never run while you still feel drunk. If you're hungover, rehydrate and eat before you lace up, keep the run short and easy, and stop if you feel dizzy, nauseous, or your heart is racing. Keep alcohol to one drink or none in the day or two before a race or key workout. After a run, rehydrate and eat first, then have a drink if you want one. And don't expect running to "burn off" alcohol, because your liver sets that pace, not your legs.

> **When to see a doctor (or stop running and get help).** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Stop running and seek medical care if** you have chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, fainting or near-fainting, confusion, or severe shortness of breath. **Get checked promptly if** you notice very dark or cola-colored urine together with severe muscle pain or weakness after a run, signs of heat illness (stopping sweating, hot dry skin, vomiting, confusion), or you can't keep fluids down. If you drink heavily most days and get shakes, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue and worth raising with a doctor. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Alcohol Affects Running Performance

To understand why a night out shows up in your next run, it helps to look at what alcohol does to the systems running depends on. None of these effects is dramatic after one drink. They stack up as the drink count rises.

### 1. Hydration

Alcohol lowers the release of vasopressin, a hormone (also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you otherwise would. Add in the sweating that comes with warm bars and dancing, and many people start the next morning a little behind on fluids.

Running is very sensitive to hydration. Even modest fluid loss makes your heart pump harder for the same pace, raises your body temperature faster, and makes everything feel more effortful. For a deeper look at how much alcohol actually dehydrates you, see our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 2. Sleep

This is the effect runners underestimate most. Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but as your body processes it during the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, and the deep and REM stages that help you recover get disrupted. You can spend eight hours in bed and still wake up under-recovered.

Poor sleep on its own is linked to higher perceived effort and lower endurance in the next day's exercise. So even if you feel fine, a night of drinking usually means you're running on a worse night's sleep than you think.

### 3. Blood sugar and fuel

Your liver normally keeps blood sugar steady during a run by releasing stored glucose and making new glucose from other building blocks (a process called gluconeogenesis). While it's busy processing alcohol, the liver gets worse at the second job. That raises the risk of low blood sugar, especially if you run first thing in the morning without breakfast or go long.

Drinking nights also tend to replace a proper carb-rich dinner with snacks or nothing at all. If you head out for a long run the next morning on low glycogen (the stored carbohydrate in your muscles and liver) and low blood sugar, you're more likely to hit the wall early, feel shaky, or get lightheaded.

### 4. Heart rate and rhythm

Many runners notice their heart rate is higher than normal for the same easy pace after a night of drinking. Dehydration, poor sleep, and the lingering effects of alcohol all push in that direction. It's common and usually harmless, but it's a good reason to run by feel or heart rate rather than pace the day after drinking.

There is a less common but more serious issue too. Binge drinking can trigger atrial fibrillation, an irregular and often fast heart rhythm, in some people. Doctors sometimes call this "holiday heart" because it shows up after heavy drinking around holidays and weekends. Endurance athletes, especially older long-time endurance athletes, also appear to have a somewhat higher baseline risk of atrial fibrillation. If you feel a fluttering, irregular, or pounding heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest after drinking, stop running and get checked. We cover this in more detail in our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

### 5. Temperature control

Alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin and interferes with your body's ability to regulate its temperature. Combined with dehydration, this makes heat illness more likely. A hungover run on a hot, humid morning is one of the riskier combinations covered in this guide.

### 6. Coordination and reaction time

While alcohol is still in your system, it slows reaction time and impairs balance and judgment. On a run, that translates into a higher risk of rolling an ankle, tripping on a curb, or misjudging traffic. Even the morning after a very late, heavy night, some people still have alcohol in their blood.

### 7. Muscle recovery

Hard runs cause small amounts of muscle damage, and your body repairs that damage in the hours and days afterward, building back slightly stronger. Research suggests alcohol interferes with this process. A frequently cited study from Australian researchers (Parr and colleagues, published in PLoS One in 2014) found that drinking a large amount of alcohol after a hard training session reduced muscle protein synthesis, the process of building new muscle protein, even when the athletes also had protein. Our guide on [alcohol and muscle recovery](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025) goes into the research in detail.

The amount used in that kind of study was well beyond a single beer. One drink after a run is unlikely to undo your training. A big night after a big session is a different story.

## Running With a Hangover: Should You?

This is the question most people actually have. The answer depends on how bad the hangover is, what kind of run you had planned, and the conditions.

### When an easy run is usually fine

For a healthy adult with a mild hangover (a dull headache, some tiredness, a dry mouth), a short, easy run can be fine and some people find it helps them feel more normal. Before you go:

- **Make sure the alcohol has cleared.** If you were drinking until 2 a.m. and woke up at 7, you may still have alcohol in your blood. Give it time.
- **Drink fluids first.** Have a glass or two of water, ideally with some sodium. An electrolyte drink or a salty snack with water both work.
- **Eat something.** A banana, toast, or a small breakfast with carbs helps steady your blood sugar.
- **Keep it easy and short.** Think 20 to 40 minutes at a conversational pace. This is not the day for intervals, tempo work, or a personal best.
- **Run a loop close to home.** That way you can cut it short if you feel bad.
- **Leave the watch pace alone.** Your heart rate will probably be higher than usual. Run by effort.

We look at the evidence on whether exercise actually speeds up hangover recovery in our guide on [whether exercise helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover). The short version is that it doesn't clear alcohol faster, but light movement can make some people feel better.

### When to skip it

Take a rest day, or swap the run for a walk, if any of these apply:

- You still feel drunk, unsteady, or foggy.
- You've been vomiting or can't keep fluids down.
- It's hot or humid out.
- You feel dizzy or lightheaded when you stand up.
- You've noticed palpitations, an irregular heartbeat, or chest discomfort.
- You had very little sleep.
- The plan was a long run, a hard workout, or a race-pace session.

There is no prize for forcing a hard session through a bad hangover. A missed easy run costs you almost nothing in fitness. A fall, a heat illness episode, or a heart rhythm scare can cost you weeks.

### What to do instead

If you skip the run, a walk, some gentle stretching, or an easy bike ride can still get you moving. Focus on rehydrating, eating proper meals, and getting to bed early. Move the key workout a day later if your schedule allows. For a practical step-by-step on fluids, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Can You Run Off Alcohol or Sweat It Out?

This is one of the most common myths among runners. Unfortunately, it doesn't work.

Your liver breaks down the vast majority of the alcohol you drink. It does so at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, though this varies with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors. Only a small percentage leaves your body unchanged through your breath, sweat, and urine. Exercise doesn't meaningfully speed up the liver's work.

So a hard run won't sober you up or make you safe to drive. What it will do is make you sweat out more water, which you may already be short on. If you feel better after a run, that's mostly from the fresh air, movement, and the fluids and food you had around it, not because you burned off the alcohol.

## Drinking the Night Before a Race

Whether it's a local 5K or a marathon you've trained months for, the night before a race deserves some thought.

### How much is too much?

There is no exact cutoff that applies to everyone. Here is a practical way to think about it:

- **One drink with dinner:** unlikely to have a noticeable effect for most runners, especially if you drink water alongside it and get to bed on time. Some runners find a glass of wine or a beer helps them relax before a big day.
- **Two or more drinks:** more likely to disrupt sleep and leave you slightly dehydrated. This starts to matter for goal races, especially longer ones.
- **A full night out:** a poor idea before any race you care about. The combination of less sleep, lower fluid levels, and lower fuel stores works against you on race day.

Keep in mind that the night before the night before (two nights out) often matters more for sleep than the night right before, because many people sleep badly before a race from nerves anyway. If you plan to drink in the days before a race, earlier in race week is better than the last 48 hours.

### Long races and hot races raise the stakes

For a marathon or half marathon, the effects of alcohol on fluid balance and fuel stores matter more than for a short race, because you're out there long enough for small deficits to grow. For races in hot or humid weather, add the effect of alcohol on temperature control. In both cases, the safest choice is to skip alcohol in the day or two before.

### What about carb-loading with beer?

Beer does contain carbohydrate, but far less than most people assume, and it comes with alcohol you don't want. If you're carb-loading for a long race, get your carbs from food: rice, pasta, bread, potatoes, and similar. Non-alcoholic beer can be a fun pre-race ritual without the downsides.

## Drinking After a Run or Race

The post-race beer is a tradition at many running events, and plenty of runners enjoy a drink after a long Sunday run. Here's how to keep it from undoing your effort.

### Is beer a good recovery drink?

Not really, though it's not a disaster in moderation. Beer contains water and a modest amount of carbohydrate, but it's low in sodium and protein. Alcohol has a mild diuretic effect, and in larger amounts it reduces muscle protein synthesis, as discussed above. So beer isn't a substitute for proper recovery.

Some research has looked at whether low-alcohol or non-alcoholic beer can work as a recovery drink, and those options are generally considered more reasonable for rehydration than regular beer. If you like the taste, non-alcoholic beer is a solid post-run choice.

### A better order of operations

If you want a drink after running, put it at the end of your recovery routine, not the start:

1. **Rehydrate first.** Drink water, ideally with some sodium, especially after long or sweaty runs.
2. **Eat a real meal.** Aim for carbs to refill glycogen and protein to support muscle repair.
3. **Then have your drink.** One or two drinks after you've eaten and rehydrated will have far less impact than drinking on an empty stomach while still dehydrated.
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per drink is a simple, easy habit.

Our guide on [drinking alcohol after a workout](/never-hungover/drinking-after-a-workout) goes into more detail on timing and how it affects your training gains. If you're curious about how electrolytes fit in, see our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol). If you track heart rate variability on a running watch, our guide to [alcohol and HRV](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-hrv) explains why your recovery score drops after a night out.

### Be careful after very long races

After a marathon or ultramarathon, your body is depleted, you may be dehydrated, and your blood sugar may be low. Alcohol hits harder in this state. People also sometimes take ibuprofen or other anti-inflammatory painkillers for sore legs after a race. Both alcohol and these painkillers can be hard on the stomach and kidneys, and the kidneys are already under stress after very long efforts. It's wise to rehydrate, eat, and wait before combining them, and check with a doctor or pharmacist if you have any kidney issues.

## Running While Drunk: Don't

It might seem obvious, but it's worth saying plainly. Running while intoxicated is a bad idea. Alcohol impairs balance, coordination, reaction time, and judgment, and it makes it harder for your body to handle heat. Running drunk raises the risk of falls, sprains, fractures, and traffic accidents, particularly at night. Events like the beer mile are popular for fun, but they're best treated as a novelty, done in a safe setting with no traffic, not as a regular training habit.

If you've been drinking, walk home with friends or get a ride. Save the run for when you're fully sober.

## Regular Drinking and Long-Term Training

Most of this guide has focused on single nights out. It's also worth looking at the bigger picture for runners who drink regularly.

### Training adaptations

Running fitness comes from consistent training plus good recovery. Regular heavier drinking can chip away at both: you're more likely to skip or shorten sessions because you feel rough, and the sessions you do complete may produce less adaptation if your sleep and muscle repair are repeatedly disrupted. The effect of an occasional drink is small. The effect of drinking heavily several nights a week can add up over a training block.

### Body weight and calories

Alcohol contains about 7 calories per gram, nearly as much as fat, and drinks often come with mixers and late-night food. For runners who are trying to manage weight for performance, drinks are an easy place for calories to creep in without much nutritional value.

### Bone health and injury

Heavy long-term drinking is linked to lower bone density, and runners already put a lot of repetitive load on their bones. This mainly applies to heavy drinkers rather than people who have the occasional drink, but it's another reason moderation pays off for runners.

### Heart health

Moderate exercise and the heart are generally a great combination. Heavy drinking is not. As mentioned above, binge drinking can trigger irregular heart rhythms, and regular heavy drinking is linked to high blood pressure and other heart problems over time. Runners aren't immune just because they're fit. For a wider look at how alcohol affects sports in general, see our guide on [alcohol and athletic performance](/never-hungover/alcohol-athletic-performance-complete-impact-analysis-2025).

## A Practical Plan for Runners Who Drink

You don't have to choose between being a runner and enjoying a drink. A few habits keep the trade-off small.

### Before you drink

- **Know your schedule.** Look at the next two days of training. If a race, long run, or key workout is coming, plan for one drink or none.
- **Eat a proper meal.** Food slows the absorption of alcohol and keeps your blood sugar steadier.
- **Start hydrated.** Have water during the afternoon, especially if you ran that day.

### While drinking

- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for each drink.
- **Pace yourself.** Your liver can only process about one standard drink an hour. Drinking faster than that means more alcohol builds up in your blood.
- **Choose lower-alcohol drinks.** Light beer, wine spritzers, or alternating with non-alcoholic options all help.
- **Set a cutoff time.** Stopping a few hours before bed gives your body time to process more of the alcohol before sleep, which can help sleep quality.

### The next morning

- **Rehydrate before anything else.** Water with some sodium, or an electrolyte drink.
- **Eat breakfast.** Carbs plus some protein.
- **Check in honestly.** Use the "when to skip it" list above.
- **Adjust the plan.** Swap a hard session for an easy one, or move it a day.

### After a race or long run

- **Recover first, celebrate second.** Water, food, then drinks.
- **Keep it moderate.** One or two drinks after a big effort is very different from a long night.

### A note on supplements

Some people take a supplement called DHM (dihydromyricetin) on nights out. DHM comes from the Japanese raisin tree, and early research, mostly in animals with limited human data, has looked at how it affects the way the body processes alcohol. There is no good evidence that DHM improves running performance, speeds recovery from training, or cancels out the effects of alcohol on sleep, hydration, or fuel. If you want to try it, think of it as a small extra on top of the basics, not a replacement for water, food, sleep, and drinking less before important runs. A straightforward single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Check with your doctor first if you take any regular medication.

## The Bottom Line

- A drink or two is unlikely to wreck an easy run for most healthy runners. Heavy drinking affects hydration, sleep, blood sugar, heart rate, temperature control, and muscle recovery.
- Never run while you still feel drunk, and don't count on running to burn off alcohol. Your liver sets the pace.
- If you're hungover, rehydrate and eat first, keep the run short and easy, and skip it if you're vomiting, dizzy, it's hot out, or your heart feels off.
- Keep alcohol to one drink or none in the 24 to 48 hours before a race or key session.
- After a run, recover first and drink second.
- Stop and get medical help for chest pain, an irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, fainting, confusion, or dark urine with severe muscle pain.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it OK to go for a run with a hangover?**

An easy, short run is usually fine for a healthy person with a mild hangover, as long as you have rehydrated, eaten something, and the alcohol has cleared your system. Keep the pace conversational and cut it short if you feel dizzy, sick, or your heart rate feels unusually high. Skip it entirely if you are vomiting, still feel drunk, it is hot out, or you have any chest pain or irregular heartbeat.

**Can you sweat out alcohol by running?**

No. Your liver breaks down the vast majority of the alcohol you drink, at a fairly fixed rate of roughly one standard drink per hour. Only a small percentage leaves through breath, sweat, and urine. Running does not speed up that process in any meaningful way, and sweating more while you are already dehydrated can make you feel worse.

**How long after drinking should I wait to run?**

There is no single official rule. At minimum, wait until the alcohol has cleared your blood, which for most people is roughly one hour per standard drink after your last drink. For hard sessions, long runs, or races, the effects on sleep, hydration, and blood sugar can linger into the next day, so many runners treat a heavy night as a reason to make the next day an easy or rest day.

**Will drinking the night before a race hurt my time?**

A single drink with dinner is unlikely to matter much for most runners. Several drinks probably will, mainly because alcohol fragments your sleep, adds to fluid loss, and can leave your blood sugar and glycogen stores lower than you'd like. For a goal race, the safest plan is to keep it to one drink or none in the 24 to 48 hours before.

**Is beer a good recovery drink after running?**

Not really. Beer does contain water and some carbohydrate, but it is low in sodium and protein, and alcohol has been shown to reduce muscle protein building after exercise when taken in large amounts. If you want a beer after a run, have water, food with protein and carbs, and some salt first, then enjoy one drink. Non-alcoholic beer is a reasonable option if you like the taste.

**Is running drunk dangerous?**

Yes. Alcohol slows reaction time, impairs balance and judgment, and makes it harder for your body to control its temperature. Running while intoxicated raises the risk of falls, sprained ankles, traffic accidents, and heat illness. Wait until you are fully sober.

**Why does my heart rate feel higher on a run after drinking?**

Alcohol and the dehydration that follows can raise your resting and exercise heart rate the next day, and poor sleep adds to it. That's why an easy pace can feel harder than usual. A higher heart rate that settles with rest is common, but a racing or irregular heartbeat that does not settle, or any chest pain, needs medical attention.

**Does DHM help runners who drink?**

There is no good evidence that DHM improves running performance or reverses the effects of alcohol on training. DHM has early research, mostly in animals, on how the body handles alcohol. Some people take it on nights out, but it does not replace hydration, food, sleep, or drinking less before important runs.
